rv.q: What makes 'Prince of Broadway' work so well is that it doesn't try to turn Mr. Prince's career into a conventional biographical narrative but instead uses his shows as stepping stones to explore the changing nature of the Broadway musical.

This affectionate tribute to the legendary producer-director Hal Prince is a slick, professionally assembled entertainment that will please devotees while providing newcomers with a solid primer on one of Broadway's most important figures.
The show will fill Broadway lovers with nostalgia and joy.
Musical theater buffs will eat it up; those looking for something more challenging, not so much.
Trying valiantly to chart that impossible journey, “Prince of Broadway” ends up taking us, well, nowhere special.
That’s the darker side of luck.
A generous, good-hearted show for fans.
It's a pleasant collection of beloved and familiar Broadway songs, but there isn't much to it.
The show functions mostly as a cautionary tale about the difficulty of anthologizing directors in a Broadway show.

Watching this production’s overtaxed ensemble perform vignettes from different musicals, in an oppressive succession of themed wigs and costumes, is like hearing a rushed raconteur drop name after famous name, without bothering to explain their significance.
Sometimes a prince comes up a pauper.
Here, it’s underpopulated and and looks cut-rate: a Prince of Broadway that would serve brilliantly as the entertainment at an honorary luncheon sponsored by, say, the Drama League.
If the wonderful confections of American musical theater thrill you, watching this show is like hanging out at Levain Bakery early in the morning, before the first customer arrives.

Jason Robert Brown’s new anthem, “Do The Work” concludes the evening on just the right note, for it sums up the career of Harold Prince, who at 90 is still up there inspiring, mentoring, producing and directing, for which we owe him so much.
Over the course of this fantastic evening, nine talented Broadway stars introduce many of Prince's works
PRINCE OF BROADWAY is at its best at such moments; when today's stars put their personal stamp on classic roles.
Overall, it's inevitably a charmer, nudging at our nostalgia, tugging at our heartstrings, clever, delightful, even poignant
Whether this fully hangs together as a Broadway show is another -- and highly debatable -- matter.
The entertainment level here is generally very high.

Ultimately, the numerous other highs and polished staging can't avoid a mishmash feel to the show as a whole.
Watching the three-song selection that is given the prime, next-to-closing slot in Prince of Broadway, I decided that I don’t really need to go back to the Majestic just yet.
Prince can't escape being a bit of a hodgepodge.
My sentiments, exactly, with Mr. Prince's latest.
This is a warm, if frustrating bran-tub, the fundamental negative—the under-baked presence of Prince himself—highlighted by a note from the amazing man himself within the show’s Playbill.
But seeing a collection of greatest hits from his productions does not a fully-satisfying Broadway show make.

It’d be easier to give unconditional love to Prince of Broadway – which is after all celebrating the best of Broadway, and bringing Prince back on Broadway — if the shows it’s excerpting were sadly neglected.
It’s not a deep dive into the mind of a master — more like, Shallow Hal.
Also dreadful is the book, by David Thompson, which has the cast impersonating Prince between numbers.
Prince of Broadway is a meandering tribute to the man and his work, told via a series of biographical anecdotes and revue-like musical numbers that don’t gel together into a coherent whole.
Perfectly enjoyable, but not the stunning blockbuster we’ve come to expect from Mr. Prince.
It does so, however, in a puzzlingly perfunctory fashion.
This pull between a third-person round of applause and first-person reflection keeps the show from ever really finding its feet.
Sadly, this show makes his work seem mostly ornamental.
It’s a career that has given birth to an unparalleled string of hits (and some misses as well), many of them sampled here deliciously, often thrillingly.
One smashingly executed number after another, variously performed by a versatile cast of nine.
For true Broadway aficionados, there perhaps couldn’t be a more ideal night at the theater than Prince of Broadway at MTC’s Samuel J. Friedman Theater.
I found the show thoroughly entertaining...by all means go.
And Tony Yazbeck tearing “The Right Girl” from Follies to shreds is worth the price of admission all by itself.
Even with its faults, 'Prince of Broadway' is an evening of sumptuous entertainment, spectacular performances, and surprising moments of beauty
It is worth see how some exceptionally fine performers lend their own brand of talent to some of the most enduring musicals in Broadway history.
Most of what's included is mostly terrific, including a dynamic first-act ending and a powerful Act Two beginning.
There are far worse ways to spend an evening than watching some of the most talented people in New York perform some of musical theatre's most iconic and beloved songs.
It takes the form of a revue at Manhattan Theatre Club’s Samuel J. Friedman Theatre that Prince has directed as a valentine to himself, abetted by co-director and choreographer Susan Stroman.

"It’s that 'artistic whole' that distinguishes the work of a great director (and producer). So, it is not surprising that an evening of knockout singing and dancing does not fully satisfy those who have experienced Prince’s 'whole'...But 'Prince on Broadway' is entertaining...

“A commendable overview of Prince’s career…There are restaged sequences from the shows, often—but not always—their ‘classic’ numbers, which tends toward imbalance…Still, great moments are scattered throughout…The cast performs with incomparable zest, even if some aren’t perfect for the roles they assay...
If this production makes people aware of that, it deepens their understanding of the best in American musical theater.
Still, Prince of Broadway is a mixed bag that theater maniacs might find worth grabbing into, for the showmanship and history it celebrates.
As entertaining as the numbers are, the production soon loses its luster and begins to get stale.

While I'm happy to hear strong performances from a strong cast in strong music from some of Harold Prince's most important musicals, storytelling, something that Hal Prince does like no one can, is just a tad absent.
Both Prince and the audience deserve a better effort than what is actually presented.
It feels a bit heartless, without a lot of subtlety and nuance.
In almost every instance, they do not reflect the brilliance of their source.

Prince of Broadway is a pointless exercise.
Frankly, in the most fundamental musical theater way, Prince of Broadway is a pure, audience-pleasing show and should be appreciated for its gleaming showmanship.

"If you’re expecting deep-rooted insights into the extraordinary producer-director Harold Prince’s life story, you’ll be sorely disappointed. But if you want to relive the musical memories of some of the hits and flops of his seven decades in theater, with a cast that will many times blow the roof off, you’ve come to the right place...
It may seem like I am being hard on 'Prince of Broadway,' but I still recommend it.
All in all, it is an entertaining, if not wholly satisfying or fulfilling evening.
Folks who go into this musical retrospective looking for insights are probably going to feel shortchanged.
That’s very likely true, but the eighty-nine-year-old master deserves better than Prince of Broadway.

cn.t: Critics find this Hal Prince retrospective entertaining but superficial, praising the talented cast and beloved songs from iconic musicals while lamenting the lack of insight into Prince's creative process and vision.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).
